rounds.text: Chandan Healthcare Ltd trades at a P/E of 21.3x [E1], which sits attractively below the broader sector benchmark of 30.95x [E6], while its EV/EBITDA of 11.38x also compares favourably to the sector's 14.3x [E11]. The business displays exceptional fundamental momentum, highlighted by a 5-year compounded profit growth of 102% [E17] and a trailing twelve-month profit growth of 32% [E19], heavily outperforming the sector median profit growth of 17.3% [E56]. Operating margins have expanded dramatically to 30% in Mar 2026 from 12% three years prior [E24], supported by a structurally increasing yearly margin trend over the last five years [E26]. Return metrics heavily validate this operational efficiency, with a robust ROCE of 22.8% [E12] and a median 3-year ROE of 25% [E22], both comfortably exceeding sector benchmarks [E10, E9]. Furthermore, a discounted cash flow valuation calculates an intrinsic value of Rs 417 per share against the current market price of Rs 238 [E39], presenting a substantial margin of safety of 42.9% [E40]. Conceded: [E46], [E30], [E47].

Despite impressive headline profit growth, Chandan Healthcare Ltd carries severe structural and cash-flow risks that the current valuation may fail to fully price in [E17, E18, E19]. Most alarmingly, the company's free cash flow has plunged into negative territory at Rs -17 Cr for Mar 2026, even while operating cash flow sits at Rs 24 Cr [E29, E30]. This cash burn coincides with a staggering 200% surge in Capital Work in Progress (CWIP) to Rs 12 Cr, signaling aggressive, debt-funded expansion that pushes borrowings up to Rs 39 Cr and stretches working capital days outward from 86.9 to a bloated 166 days [E33, E34, E47]. Compounding these operational warning signs, smart money is actively fleeing the counter; foreign institutional holdings have collapsed by 3.85 percentage points down to a negligible 0.01%, and domestic institutions have simultaneously trimmed their stake by 1.23 percentage points [E36, E37]. Furthermore, despite reporting repeated profits, the company offers a 0.00% dividend yield and is explicitly flagged for its zero payout policy [E4, E46]. Conceded: the company trades at a P/B of 3.5x against a sector benchmark of 3.3x, representing a minor premium, but one largely supported by a strong ROCE of 22.8% [E7, E12].

Conceded: free cash flow sits at Rs -17 Cr for Mar 2026 [E30], and working capital days have increased to 166 days [E47]. However, this cash burn is directly attributable to a +200% surge in CWIP to Rs 12 Cr [E34], which represents growth-oriented capex that will power future earnings rather than structural deterioration. Conceded: borrowings have risen to Rs 39 Cr [E33], but the debt-to-equity ratio remains a healthy and conservatively financed 0.23x [E32]. Conceded: institutional divestments occurred [E36, E37], but overall institutional money flow is currently registering as POSITIVE MONEY FLOW with a slight holding increase [E38]. Conceded: the dividend yield is 0.00% [E4], but the zero payout is actively funding the high-return capital deployment driving an exceptional 22.8% ROCE [E12]. Finally, the minor P/B premium of 3.5x against the sector benchmark of 3.3x [E7] is entirely justified by a superior ROCE of 19.64% [E10] and ROE of 15.82% [E9] beating sector benchmarks of 14.79% and 11.94% respectively.

Conceded: the debt-to-equity ratio sits at a conservatively financed 0.23x [E32], and the ROCE of 19.64% beats the sector benchmark of 14.79% [E10]. However, dismissing the negative free cash flow of Rs -17 Cr as mere growth-oriented capex ignores the severe operational drain shown by working capital days worsening dramatically from 86.9 to 166 days [E30, E47]. While the bull points to a +200% surge in CWIP [E34] to justify this cash burn, borrowings have simultaneously expanded to Rs 39 Cr [E33], and the 0.00% dividend yield leaves minority shareholders funding this capital-intensive expansion without any direct cash returns [E4]. Furthermore, the claim of positive institutional money flow is undermined by heavy, direct institutional divestment, with foreign holdings plunging from 3.86% to 0.01% and domestic institutions cutting their stake from 6.32% to 5.09% [E36, E37]. Finally, this insider and institutional flight coincides with a 1-year share price return of -5% [E20], demonstrating that the market remains unconvinced by the sustainability of these margins despite the historical profit growth [E17, E24].
